text:
Alter it, beginning by ending the ranking’s power to exclude members from the workstations. Keep the dashboard as a limited record of contributions if members find it useful.

The decisive detail is that there is nowhere else to use the equipment. A score presented as recognition has become permission to participate. The coordinators enforce a definition of contribution that misses at least some of what sustains the cooperative. People must satisfy that definition even when doing so distracts them from the work itself. Calling the arrangement member-run does not resolve this.

Still, the members who feel newly visible have identified something worth preserving. Teaching and cleaning can disappear easily from accounts of who does the work. Abolishing their record could restore that invisibility.

I would propose a six-week trial within the existing budget and categories:

- Restore equipment eligibility to members below the threshold. Allocate scarce workstation time through transparent booking limits and a rotating priority rule that members can challenge.
- Retain the contribution record without an access cutoff or competitive ranking. Make its acknowledged gaps explicit.
- Agree on workable teaching, maintenance and cleaning responsibilities, with ways to swap tasks and raise difficulties privately. Necessary work still has to happen.

Gather responses in writing as well as at a meeting, so attendance does not determine whose experience counts. Review whether tools are maintained, novices supported and access fairly shared. The dashboard should help members organize those activities; they should not have to organize their activities around surviving the dashboard.
